analysis.one_liner: Requires large employers to extend health coverage, family leave, and pension credit to part-time workers.
analysis.headline: The Part-Time Worker Bill of Rights never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to four House committees in February 2013 and sat there until the Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require large employers to treat part-time workers more like full-time ones. It would extend the health-coverage mandate under the Affordable Care Act to part-time employees, with the penalty prorated by hours worked [S2] [S3]. It would let part-time workers qualify for family and medical leave after 12 months with an employer, without the current 1,250-hour work requirement [S2] [S3]. And it would let employees who work 500 or more hours a year earn credit toward joining, vesting in, and accruing benefits under employer pension plans [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Part-time and temporary workers — disproportionately women, students, and people cobbling together jobs — who today can be denied employer health coverage, unpaid family leave, and pension credit because they fall short of full-time thresholds. Around 28 million Americans work part time involuntarily, and millions more work part time by choice; all would gain access to benefits they now lose. Workers at staffing and leasing firms would also gain ERISA protections for the first time.

how_it_helps.text: Extends the ACA large-employer health coverage mandate to part-time employees, so a large employer that does not offer coverage owes a penalty per employee, prorated to hours worked, rather than only per full-time employee [S2] [S3].
Removes the 1,250-hour service requirement from the Family and Medical Leave Act, making any employee with 12 months on the job eligible for protected unpaid family and medical leave [S2] [S3].

Under ERISA pension rules, employees customarily working 500 or more hours per year would be treated as meeting the 1,000-hour threshold for plan participation, vesting, and benefit accrual [S2] [S3].
Extends ERISA protections to certain leased and contracted workers, a group largely outside employer benefit law today [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large employers — especially retail, restaurant, and staffing companies that keep much of their workforce under 30 hours a week — would bear new costs: prorated health-coverage penalties for uncovered part-timers, family-leave obligations for far more workers, and pension participation and vesting for anyone working 500 hours or more a year. Some employers would respond by cutting hours, shifting jobs, or raising prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill would raise labor costs at exactly the firms that rely on part-time scheduling, and an honest supporter should acknowledge the risk that employers respond by trimming hours, converting jobs to subcontracting, or raising prices rather than simply absorbing the cost.

Because the penalty for an uncovered part-timer is prorated to hours worked, the per-worker cost is lower than for a full-timer, but the covered workforce would be much larger, making the aggregate cost to affected industries substantial.

The pension provisions hinge on what a position 'customarily' requires, which would create fact-specific disputes and regulatory paperwork for plan administrators and for workers trying to prove their hours.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real and aimed at a large, long-ignored group: workers under full-time thresholds get no employer health coverage, no family leave, and often no pension credit no matter how many years they show up. The costs fall on large employers, whose incentive to keep workers under 30 hours a week is precisely what this bill targets. The design is reasonably careful — penalties prorated by hours, phase-ins for union plans — but the employer-response risk is genuine and unaddressed in the bill text. On balance, this is a substantial, well-aimed transfer of security to part-time workers at real cost to their employers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to four House committees and then to two subcommittees, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Janice Schakowsky introduced the Part-Time Worker Bill of Rights Act on February 13, 2013 [S1] [S5].

It was referred to four committees at once — Education and the Workforce, Ways and Means, House Administration, and Oversight and Government Reform — a structure in which each committee only considers the pieces in its jurisdiction and any one of them can keep the bill from moving [S5].
On April 23, 2013, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections and the Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
No further action was ever taken; there was no committee vote, no floor vote, and no Senate companion activity recorded before the Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S5] [S1].
The bill drew 17 cosponsors, all House Democrats [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large employers that rely heavily on part-time labor — retail, restaurant, and staffing companies — are better off, because they never had to face the new coverage, leave, and pension obligations. The House majority that controlled the committees is also better off in the sense that a bill expanding employer obligations never advanced. Part-time workers, the intended beneficiaries, gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: Every recorded supporter — the sponsor and all 17 cosponsors — was a House Democrat, and the Republican chairs who controlled the four committees the bill sat in took no action; the bill never reached the point of a roll-call vote.

industries.industry: Large employers of part-time labor (retail, restaurants, hospitality)
industries.note: These firms would owe prorated health-coverage penalties for uncovered part-timers, family-leave eligibility for workers with 12 months on the job, and pension participation for anyone working 500 hours or more a year. Their business model of keeping workers under full-time thresholds to avoid benefit costs is exactly what the bill is designed to close off.
The bill extends ERISA coverage to certain leased and contracted workers, narrowing the main advantage of leasing arrangements — keeping workers off the employer's benefit rolls.

industries.industry: Employer health insurers and benefits administrators
industries.note: Millions of additional part-time workers would become candidates for employer-sponsored coverage, expanding the pool of covered lives. The gain only materializes if employers choose to offer coverage rather than pay the prorated penalty.
